ta-l1d36q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 36. Having shown that God knows all things, so that things are said to be in God, Lombard asks how known things are in God the knower, and then (Dist. 37) how God is in things. He asks whether all God knows can be said to be in his essence (no), then whether all things, even evils, are simply in God, answering and confirming that to be in God is the same as to be from him and through him, so evils are not in him; he distinguishes 'from him', 'through him', and 'in him' as referred to the persons, and 'de ipso' from 'ex ipso'; and he concludes that all things are in God's knowledge or foreknowledge. Thomas asks two questions, on what God knows and on the ideas by which he knows. On the first, three articles: whether God knows singulars; whether he knows evils; and how what he knows is in him.
claims: Evils are in God's knowledge but not in God, since they are not from him.
concepts: ex ipso, per ipsum, in ipso

ta-l1d36q1-d1e131.summary: First argument that God does not know singulars. Boethius says the universal is while understood, the particular while sensed, and God has no sensitive power, which is a power in a bodily organ.
claims: Singulars are known by sense.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e134.summary: Second argument. Something is known only as it is in the knower, and particular effects are in universal causes only potentially, and the divine essence, in which God knows all, is the universal cause.
claims: Particulars are potential in universal causes.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e137.summary: Third argument. Knowledge is by assimilation, and the singular is singular only by matter, so no power abstracting from matter knows the singular as such, and the divine intellect is most separate from matter.
claims: Singularity is by matter.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e141.summary: Fourth argument. Dionysius says creatures participate God's one goodness as many lines come from one centre and many impressions from one seal, but knowing the centre one knows the lines only in common, not as this or that.
claims: Knowing the centre does not give knowledge of each line.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e144.summary: Sed contra from Heb. 11:6: whoever approaches God must believe that he is and rewards those who seek him, and he cannot reward singular human works without knowing the agents and their works.
claims: God rewards singular works.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e150.summary: Second sed contra. God has practical knowledge of things, the principle of operation, and operation concerns singulars.
claims: Practical knowledge concerns singulars.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e153.summary: Thomas's determination. God undoubtedly knows all things, universal and singular, though opinions differ. The Commentator (Metaphysics 11) seems to deny God knowledge of particulars except as he knows his essence, principle of all being; but God causes not only things' being but all that is in them, so he knows them not only as beings but as such and such. Avicenna and Algazel say God knows singulars universally: as one knowing all distances and motions of orbs and planets would foresee every eclipse but not this eclipse as this, except through sense, but universally, by its causes, so God, knowing himself, knows all secondary causes and their effects, but only universally, the determination being on the side of the known, not only of the knower (on the knower's side it is true that God does not know particulars by particular knowledge, Dist. 35). This is insufficient, since knowing the singular in the universal is not knowing its proper nature, as no aggregation of universals makes a singular except by individuation through matter, so universal causes lead only to knowing a particular's common nature. Rabbi Moses says God knows singulars perfectly and answers all objections by holding God's knowledge equivocal with ours, so nothing can be argued from ours, as Isa. 55 says ('as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways above yours'). This is true, but more must be said, since through our knowledge we reach God's somehow, so it is analogical (Dist. 35), and we must say how ours imitates his, where and why it falls short, and so answer the arguments. So we proceed by Dionysius's way: since God knows things by his essence, which causes them, he knows them in the way he gave them being, so if anything in things were unknown to him, divine operation would be absent there. The philosophers had difficulty because some held that God does not act immediately in all things but produces first things through which others are produced, so they could find no way he knows things here except in first universal causes; and some held matter was not made, God acting only by inducing form, and since matter individuates, they could not explain how God knows singulars as such. Since we hold that God acts immediately in all things and that from him are not only formal principles but matter, he knows by his essence as cause all that is in a thing, formal and material, and so knows things not only by universal natures but as individuated by matter, as a builder who could produce the whole house, matter and form, by the art-form in his mind would know this house and that by it, whereas since his art induces only form, it is a likeness of the form only and he knows this house only through sense.
claims: God knows singulars as singular, against Averroes and against Avicenna's 'universal' knowledge of singulars.
Because God creates matter and acts immediately in all things, his essence as cause is a likeness of the whole thing, form and matter.
God's knowledge is analogical, not equivocal, against Maimonides.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the first argument. The form by which the divine intellect understands is neither universal, since it receives no additions, nor singular, since it is free of matter, but is the principle and perfect likeness of all that is in a thing, matter and form. So 'the universal while understood, the particular while sensed' concerns our knowledge, in sense by a material form and in intellect by a universal form, so we know particulars only by a power in which something is particularly; but God knows particulars neither universally nor particularly on the side of the knower, but universally and particularly on the side of the known.
claims: God's medium is neither universal nor particular but a perfect likeness of the whole thing.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the second argument. Particulars cannot be perfectly known in universal causes that are not their whole cause, but God is the universal cause of all as perfect cause of each, so knowing himself he knows all perfectly.
claims: God is the perfect cause of each thing.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the third argument. Though nothing in God is material and his essence is pure act, that act causes all that is in things, material and formal, and everything and whatever is in it imitates that act as far as it can, so the divine essence is the likeness of material as well as formal aspects and through it singulars can be known as such.
claims: God's act is the likeness of matter too.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. All examples from creatures applied to God fall short (Dionysius), since no common cause in creatures causes all that is in a thing, as a seal causes the figure in wax but not the wax, so knowing the seal does not give knowledge of the impressed figure as this or that, which it has from matter.
claims: No creaturely cause is total, so the analogies fail.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e181.summary: First argument that God does not know evils. The Commentator says an intellect always in act does not know privation at all, and evil is privation (Augustine).
claims: An intellect always in act does not know privation.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e184.summary: Second argument. All knowledge causes or is caused by its objects, and God's is not caused, and he is not the cause of evils.
claims: God's knowledge causes its objects.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e187.summary: Third argument. Knowledge is assimilation to the known, and evil as such is not assimilated to God but is departure from likeness to him.
claims: Evil is unlike God.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument, against knowing evil through good. Knowing something through another, not through itself, is imperfect knowledge, which is not to be attributed to God.
claims: Indirect knowledge is imperfect.
concepts: per se vs. per aliud knowledge

ta-l1d36q1-d1e194.summary: Sed contra from Ps. 68:6, 'God, you know my folly, and my offences are not hidden from you'.
claims: God knows sins.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e200.summary: Second sed contra. The straight is judge of itself and the crooked (the Philosopher), and evil is a deviation from the straightness of good, so God, who knows all goods perfectly, knows evil.
claims: The straight judges the crooked.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e203.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Not to know' is said two ways. Metaphorically, by likeness to one who does not know: God's reprobating is called not knowing, since he excludes the wicked from his glory as one excludes strangers from his secrets, and conversely he is said to know what he approves; in this sense God does not know evils. Properly, it means lacking knowledge of a thing, and so God knows goods and evils by knowing his essence, as darkness is known by knowing light (Dionysius). A privation is known only through its opposite habit, and is opposed to a habit only in the same subject. Since the light of the divine essence cannot fail, no privation is opposed to it, so evil is not opposed to good as it is determinately in God, though perhaps to the common intention of good; it is opposed determinately to the good participated in creatures, which can be mixed with defect. So by knowing his essence God knows what is from him, and through these their defects; if he knew only his essence he would know evil or privation only in common.
claims: God does not 'know' evils metaphorically (he does not approve them) but knows them properly through the goods they deprive.
Evil is opposed to participated good in creatures, not to God's good.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e206.summary: This answers the first argument: because the Commentator holds that God knows only his essence, it follows that he does not know evils, as he adds that God does not know evils exist. In the way God knows other things he knows their privations, not as first understood, since no privation can be in his intellect, but as second understood (Dist. 35).
claims: God knows privations as second objects.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the second argument. God's knowledge is in no way caused by things, but it is not the cause of all it knows, only of what it knows per se, goods; it knows evils through goods.
claims: God's knowledge causes goods; evils are known through goods.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the third argument. God knows evil not by its likeness but by the likeness of good: knowing his essence he knows each thing as far as it participates his goodness and where it falls short, and so knows evil, which consists in defect.
claims: Evil is known through the good's likeness and the defect from it.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Knowing through another what is naturally knowable through itself is imperfect, but evil has no cause, will, or knowledge of itself, only through good (Dionysius), so knowing evil through good is perfect knowledge of it.
claims: Evil is perfectly known through good.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e228.summary: First argument that what God knows is not in God. Whatever has something diverse from it in it is composite, and God is most simple.
claims: Diverse things in God would compose him.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e231.summary: Second argument, against 'in God by likeness'. A thing is more truly where it is by essence than where it is by likeness, which is only in some respect, so things would be more truly in themselves than in God, against Augustine and Anselm.
claims: Things are truer in themselves than in likeness.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e234.summary: Third argument. A likeness corresponds to what it is the likeness of, and not all things have light and life, while in God they are life and light, so they are not in God by likeness.
claims: Likeness should match the original.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e238.summary: Fourth argument. Where a thing is by likeness its proper operation is not attributed to it (a stone in the eye does not fall), but Acts 17 says in God we live, move, and are.
claims: In God we live and move.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e241.summary: Fifth argument. The likenesses of things in God's knowledge, pertaining to knowledge, are appropriated to the Son, but 'in him' is appropriated in the text to the Spirit ('through him' to the Son, 'from him' to the Father).
claims: Ideas belong to the Son, but 'in him' to the Spirit.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e244.summary: Sed contra from John 1:3–4, 'what was made in him was life'.
claims: Things are life in the Word.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e250.summary: Thomas's determination. 'In' signifies different relations with different terms, so being in God's knowledge, in God, and in the divine essence differ. 'Knowledge' names cognition, so being in God's knowledge is being known by it, and all God knows, good and evil, is in his knowledge. 'Essence' is signified as form or nature, so being in the divine essence is subsisting in or being the same as the divine nature, so creatures are not in the divine essence, only the persons, properties, and attributes. 'God' signifies a subsistent thing that is and operates, so being in God means either being in his being, and creatures are not so in God, or being subject to his work, as we say the works we are masters of are in us, and so all that is from God is in him, but not evils, which are not from him. These three are ordered: whatever is in the divine essence is in God, as pertaining to his being, but not conversely, since what is subject to his work is in him but not in his essence; and whatever is in God is in his knowledge, but not conversely, as with evils.
claims: Being in God's knowledge, in God, and in his essence are distinct and ordered.
Creatures are in God as subject to his work, not in his essence; evils are only in his knowledge.
concepts: esse in scientia, in Deo, in essentia

ta-l1d36q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the first argument. Nothing in God is diverse from him, so creatures as in God are not other than God, since creatures in God are the creative essence (Anselm): they are in God by their likeness, and the divine essence is the likeness of all that is from God.
claims: Creatures in God are the creative essence.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e256.summary: Reply to the second argument. A creature's being can be considered in its own nature, in our knowledge, in God, or commonly, abstracting from these. 'The creature has truer being in God than in itself' compares the first and third with respect to the fourth, since every comparison is by something common: in God it has truer being because whatever is in something is in it in that thing's mode, so in God it is by uncreated being and in itself by created being, which has less truth of being. Compared to being in our soul, being in its own nature exceeds as substantial over accidental and is exceeded as material by intellectual, so sometimes a thing has truer being where it is by likeness than in itself.
claims: Things have truer being in God, since they are there by uncreated being.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the third argument. A likeness in the soul can be considered as likeness of the thing, and then only what is in the thing is attributed to it, or by the being it has in the soul, and then intelligibility or universality are attributed to it, as a stone image is stone by its subject, not by its original. So the likeness of things in God is life and light not as likeness but as in God: life as principle of operation to the being of things (as the Philosopher calls the heavens' motion a life for all natural things), light as principle of knowing things. Or the likeness in the soul is called life as a form and perfection of intellect and light as principle of intellectual operation, and so things in God are life and light, being in him as artefacts in the artisan by their likenesses.
claims: Ideas are life and light by their being in God, not as likenesses.
concepts: likeness as likeness vs. as being

ta-l1d36q1-d1e263.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Being, living, and moving are attributed to things not by their being in God but by the being they have in themselves from God (being pertaining to essence, living to power, moving to operation; or living to soul, moving to body, being to both), so things existing in their own nature are said to be in God as their being is contained by God, and likewise their motion and life.
claims: We live and move in God as contained by him.

ta-l1d36q1-d1e266.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The likeness of a thing in God is not taken from the thing but causes it, so whatever is in him by likeness is in him as in an operating and conserving principle, and operation and conservation are completed by his will and goodness, will being nearest to the work among knowledge, power, and will. So 'in him' is appropriated to the Spirit, who proceeds by way of will and to whom goodness is appropriated, since 'in' says the relation of containing and conserving; 'through him' to the Son, since 'per' denotes formal cause and art, the artisan's form of working, is appropriated to the Son; 'from him' to the Father, since 'ex' implies principle, and he is principle not from a principle.
claims: 'Ex ipso, per ipsum, in ipso' are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit as principle, formal art, and conserving will.

ta-l1d36q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 36 divides Lombard's treatment of how known things are in God, denying that evils are in God, and announces two questions, on what God knows and on the ideas, with three articles on singulars, evils, and how known things are in God.
claims: Evils are in God's knowledge, not in God.

ta-l1d36q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 holds that God knows singulars as singular. Against Averroes, his causality extends to all that is in things; against Avicenna and Algazel, universal knowledge of singulars does not reach their proper natures; and against Maimonides' equivocity, his knowledge is analogical. Because God creates matter and acts immediately in all things, his essence is a likeness of the whole thing, form and matter, unlike a builder's art. His medium is neither universal nor particular, and no creaturely analogy is adequate.
claims: God knows singulars through his essence as cause of their matter and form.

ta-l1d36q1-Dd1e173.summary: Article 2 holds that God knows evils properly, though not in the metaphorical sense of approving them, through the goods they deprive, since evil is opposed to participated good in creatures. He knows privations as second objects, and knowing evil through good is perfect knowledge of it, since evil has no knowability of its own.
claims: God knows evils through the goods they deprive.

ta-l1d36q1-Dd1e220.summary: Article 3 distinguishes being in God's knowledge (all known things, including evils), in God (all that is from him, as subject to his work), and in his essence (only persons, properties, attributes). Creatures in God are the creative essence and have truer being there. Ideas are life and light by their being in God, and 'from him, through him, in him' are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit.
claims: Creatures are in God as subject to his work and have truer being there; evils are only in his knowledge.
concepts: esse in scientia, in Deo, in essentia

ta-l1d36q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 36 treats what God knows. Article 1 holds, against Averroes, Avicenna, and Maimonides, that God knows singulars as singular, since as creator of matter and immediate agent his essence is a likeness of the whole thing. Article 2 holds that he knows evils through the goods they deprive. Article 3 distinguishes being in God's knowledge, in God, and in his essence: creatures are in God as subject to his work and truer there, while evils are only in his knowledge.
claims: God knows singulars and evils through his essence.
Creatures are in God as subject to his work; evils only in his knowledge.
